Good afternoon. Good afternoon. Please take your seats. Last welcoming at the door after summer break. Good to see many ambassadors back. Welcome. I hope you all had a good summer break. But In this House, we never have a break. Therefore, I call to order the informal meeting to conduct an interactive dialogue with Mr. Olara Otunnu, candidate for the position of the United Nations Secretary-General. Today's interactive dialogue marks a critical step in the selection and appointment process for the next Secretary-General, while also coming at a pivotal moment for the United Nations. The person we select will be more than the face of this institution. Our choice will send a powerful message about who we are and whether we truly serve all 8 billion people of the world in all their diversity. The multilateral system, with the United Nations at its center, is under unprecedented political and financial pressure. from a deepening liquidity crisis to fundamental principles of the United Nations Charter being put into question. The next Secretary-General will be entrusted not only with navigating these challenges, but also with advancing essential reforms to ensure the United Nations is fit for the future. At the same time, the world needs the United Nations more than ever. And it needs a Secretary-General who can provide strong, principled and effective leadership across all three pillars: peace and security, development and human rights. These interactive dialogues, which I convene in line with General Assembly resolution 79/327, offer a unique opportunity for candidates to present their vision for the future of this Organization. and for Member States and civil society to ask questions and interact directly with candidates. The interactive dialogues are essential to ensuring a transparent and inclusive selection and appointment process while underlining the important role of the General Assembly. I encourage you to make full use of this opportunity, and I thank all candidates for their active participation, Member States and civil society for their questions and engagement. But these dialogues do not end in this chamber. They are also an opportunity for people around the world, the very people the United Nations serves, to listen, to engage, and to hold this process to the highest standards. For this decision does not only concern a few, but all of us in and outside the United Nations, and who look to this institution to reflect the principles and values it champions. As reflected in my latest dated 4th March, April 15th, and August 6th, 2026, the dialogue will begin with an introduction by the candidate of their vision and priorities for up to 10 minutes, followed by an interactive exchange. Each interactive dialogue will last up to three hours. The interactive exchange will take place in two segments, as we have practiced many times before. We will begin with a one and a half hour discussion focused on leadership abilities, experience, and skills needed to lead a strong organization that is fit for the future. Following this, we will move into the second segment, which will focus on the three pillars of the United Nations, peace and security, development, and human rights. In line with revitalization resolution, civil society representatives will be invited to pose question in each of the two thematic segments. Before proceeding to hear the presentation of the vision of candidate, I would like to inform Members on how to inscribe to speak in the two thematic segments. Delegations wishing to speak can register their wish to speak by pressing the microphone button. Please do not press the microphone button yet. I will announce when delegation will be asked to press the microphone button at the beginning of the first segment. Member States speaking on behalf of a group are invited to approach the list of speakers table and will be given priority. Delegations can speak only once in each segment, whether on behalf of a group or in national capacity. In the second segment, priority will be given to delegations that did not have an opportunity to speak during the first segment. Now, I invite Mr. Otunnu to present his vision. Please, Your Excellency, the floor is yours.

Your Excellencies, Madame la Presidente.

Madam President of the General Assembly, distinguished ambassadors, esteemed delegates, members of civil society. Madam President, I thank you for organizing this dialogue and for giving me the opportunity to engage with you. I would like to thank the Secretary-General as well as the staff of the United Nations for their dedication and service to the organization. Our tribute to them is all the more poignant today on the anniversary of the deaths of 22 United Nations staff in the August 2003 bombing of the UN offices in Baghdad. Among those killed were two of my dear friends, Sergio Vera de Mello of Brazil and Nadia Younis of Egypt. and one of the survivors, Mr. Salim Lone of Kenya, is with us today in this very chamber. I also wish to salute my colleagues and fellow candidates for their commitment and their offer to serve the United Nations. Madam President, In the UN Charter, there is a focus on this solemn commitment. We, the people of the United Nations, are resolved to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war, to reaffirm our faith in fundamental human rights, in the dignity and worth of the human person, to ensure the equality of rights between men and women, as well as between great and small nations, to establish the conditions for justice, and to promote social progress, as well as to ensure better standards of life in larger freedom. It is upon the bedrock of this collective pledge that the three pillars of the UN's work are built. That is to say, peace and security, human rights, and sustainable development. We must continue to work substantively on all of these pillars. The United Nations is the only body that represents all of humanity. It was founded in the aftermath of a brutal global war and against the backdrop of the Holocaust to promote international cooperation and to foster the settlement of international disputes by peaceful means. At no time has this mission been more essential than today. We are living at a time of profound upheaval and radical changes, marked by grave threats to international peace and security. There is growing fragmentation of the global economy, and deep economic fractures. There is a wavering consensus on the fundamental principles of human rights. Crucial issues linked to climate and environment are arising at a time when autonomous systems and artificial intelligence may evolve to dominate the human race. And yet with rapid advances in the field of AI, together with other major advances and profound transformations in science and technology, this may lead to a golden age in human history, a time in which hitherto incurable diseases could be prevented or cured, a time to lift billions of people out of poverty through financial and digital inclusion. It is against this backdrop of hope and of great promise, as well as of growing threats, that the United Nations, once again, is called upon to fulfill its historic charge.

Even though we must keep our view firmly on the three pillars of UN action, From time to time, the flow of events will shape priorities and emphasis. Today, we are in a situation of major conflicts around the globe. These conflicts must constitute a particular priority for the Secretary-General, engaged, present, probing, listening, seeking opportunities to suggest a way out, all recognizing that in the end, the decision will be on the part of the parties in conflict and the major players. I especially have in mind the conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza, the Great Lakes region of Africa, Sudan, Iran, the Horn of Africa, the Sahel. One of the most disturbing features of the situations I refer to is the fact that innocent civilians, particularly women and children, are disproportionately affected by these conflicts. It is one of the reasons why we cannot stand still we must do everything within our powers to act. Over the years, we have continued to emphasize the importance of human rights. In the words of the Charter, fundamental human rights and the dignity and worth of the human person. These are the words of the Charter. And we must return to the basics in terms of the regime of human rights of which I speak, the basics as postulated in the charter. For a human rights approach to be credible and enjoy broad legitimacy, every effort must be made to guard against politicization, instrumentalization, and the intrusion of ideology in our pursuit of human rights. There should be greater sensitivity to different cultural perspectives and social norms. The UN must better understand and acknowledge the deep traditions and cultures of human dignity, respect, and social cohesion that exist in many societies. This in part would be my approach for rebuilding consensus on the issue of human rights back to the basics. For the United Nations to discharge the responsibility set out in the charter, let me say this clearly and simply, reform is no longer an optional choice. It is an imperative. Without it, the institution is at grave risk. We cannot continue to do business as usual. To do so would be a grave mistake and error of judgment. Key to the organization's success is its legitimacy, effectiveness, and efficiency. And therefore, the reform initiative subsumed under UN80 must not only be continued as a priority of the Secretary-General, but be a continuous process that becomes part of the DNA, the outlook, the culture of the organization. Every organization that wishes to be on the cutting edge, vibrant and viable, must consistently bring review and constantly. Madam President, as Secretary-General, I would put priority on harnessing the incredible force which is being unleashed by artificial intelligence to make this a force for good for the entire world community with access and benefit for all. I have, over the last five years, been based in northern Uganda, and when the calls and messages asking me to consider to be a candidate for this position came, I was in northern Uganda. What was I doing there? Many of you will recall this is a part of the world that was radically destroyed, collapsed as a result of over 20 years of the LRA war. So I've been engaged with others in the enterprise of rebuilding of restoring, of resuscitating a terribly broken society. I have some idea what peace building means at the ground level. And I believe that United Nations should make it its business to enunciate policies and standards from New York and Geneva and Vienna, but also follow to see the impact on the ground at the national and community level. And finally, Madam President, what I offer if I'm given the opportunity to be Secretary-General is broad and very deep experience of working across all the three pillars of the UN. It is a track record of building consensus and offering innovative solutions in times of deadlock and crisis. And I would just, Madam President, please end on this note because this inspires me. It is Saint Francis of Assisi. "Lord, make me an instrument of your peace. Where there is hatred, let me sow love. Where there is injury, pardon. Where there is doubt, faith. Where there is despair, hope. Where there is darkness, light. Where there is sadness, joy. I would embrace this role with the same passion, commitment that I've shown in every leadership position I've had here. I thank you very much, Madam President.

I thank Mr. Otunnu. We now proceed to the first segment. Delegation wishing to speak in the first segment are invited to press the microphone button now. Members are reminded that they are encouraged to ask short and focused questions. The response should not be more than two minutes for questions from delegations speaking in national capacity, and not more than three minutes from delegations speaking on behalf of a group of Member States. I will remind candidates, I would remind you, Mr. Otunnu, also to stick to your speaking time limits. I will hand you over a card. You don't have automatic microphone cut-offs, but to have a fair and transparent process for everybody else, I would kindly ask you to stay within the time limit. Civil society questions will be interspersed with questions from Member States. As mentioned before, we will now focus on leadership abilities, experience and skills needed to lead a strong organization that is fit for the future. As the first speaker, I now give the floor to the distinguished representative from Qatar on behalf of the Arab Group, followed by the European Union and Nepal.

Thank you, Madam President. We are honored to speak on behalf of the Arab Group, and we thank Mr. Ollar-Otuna for presenting his vision and priorities for this position. We reaffirm our availability to work with the candidate to enhance the organization's ability to deal with the current challenges and to further establish sustainable development and the UN Charter principles. We have the following questions. First, with regards to the differences in the implementation of international law between countries. What do you think about the issue of non-selectiveness in order to enhance the credibility of the multilateral system and enhance the reliability of these standards? Second, how will you work on increasing the effectiveness of the efforts of the organization with regards to the question of Palestine in order to implement relevant resolutions and obtain a sustainable peace, sustaining peace? Third, we see an increase in conflicts and challenges related to the respect of international law and to the UN Charter. How do you propose that this adherence should be strengthened and to enable UN organizations such as UNRWA from fulfilling their roles? Fourth, as for the liquidity crisis and the regression in development efforts and the issue of rising debt, how will you work on the development pillar and advance the implementation of the UN Sustainable Development Agenda and provide help for developing countries? Fifth, what is your opinion on the reform of the Security Council? Which mechanism do you think would be most effective, and what is your opinion also on expansion of the Security Council and the use of veto six. How do you, what do you see, how do you view the UN 80 initiative and its possibility and effects on the organization? Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Qatar on behalf of the Arab group. Just a reminder for everybody, we have three hours. You can also come back to some of the questions if it's not possible in the time limits. Please, Mr. Otunur, you have the floor.

First, on the reform of the Security Council, very important project, very historic project. The primary responsibility falls on Member States, especially the permanent members and the other members of the Organization, to continue working, discussing, and come up with a consensus that is viable. But as Secretary-General, I would very much encourage this. and underscore the fact that there's some historical imbalance that needs to be corrected, but there should be a consensus that is forged between the permanent members and the rest of the membership. Development continues to be exceedingly important, and indeed, I'm concerned that we don't seem to be on track on current indications for fulfilling the SDGs. particular emphasis should be put on garnering more resources, on encouraging developing countries to assume more responsibility within their own countries so that we perform better on the SDGs than we did on the Millennium Development Goals, with which I was very much involved. On the UN Charter and the principles in the UN Charter, These principles are for the entire United Nations and the entire membership. And indeed, they should be applied, they should be invoked, they should be promoted without any selectivity whatsoever. That goes for our promotion of human rights, broadly speaking. It goes for promotion of international law, broadly speaking. We should go back to the basics, I said earlier, but once at the basics, we should not be selective in the application of these values and norms. Thank you. Yes, on Gaza and Palestine, you heard me say that among the conflicts on which I would focus immediately because of the unacceptable level of suffering and and uh tragedy is the Gaza situation but we should not stop at ending the current phase of the conflict is exceedingly important that we begin as a matter of priority to address the root cause of the problem and have a long-term solution to this problem. I say a little bit more in my little vision statement on this matter. Thank you.
I thank Mr. Otunnu. I now give the floor to the Distinguished Representative of the European Union on behalf of the EU and its Member States.

Thank you, Madam President, and thank you, Mr. Otunnu, for sharing your vision with us today. I have the honor to speak on behalf of the European Union and its Member States. At this critical juncture, the United Nations needs a Secretary-General who can build trust, reduce polarization, and bridge divides. Someone who can mobilize collective action, accelerate UN reforms, and deliver solutions that make a real difference in people's lives on the ground. It also needs a Secretary-General that is fully prepared to defend and promote full respect for the UN Charter and international law, and all three pillars equally. We emphasize this last point because the EU's support to the UN reflects precisely that premise. We support all strengths of the UN's work equally. On peace and security, we actively advance the implementation of key UN mandates through our security and defense missions around the world. On sustainable development, we provide close to 50% of all ODA and over one third of all voluntary contributions to the UN system. safeguarding the SDGs and battling inequality. And on human rights, we are committed to protecting and defending all human rights, civil and political, economic, social and cultural, with equal vigor. And we are therefore deeply concerned with recent normative attacks on human rights, including on women's and girls' full enjoyment of human rights and on gender equality, as well as racial, religious, political and other forms of discrimination and persecution, and also with the fact that, remarkably, only 1% of the UN system spending is dedicated to human rights mandates. It's a clear imbalance between the three UN pillars. So against this backdrop, I'd like to ask the following question. As Secretary-General, how would you plan to protect and increase the funding of the human rights pillar as explicitly mandated in the Pact for the Future? And I thank you.
I thank the Distinguished Representative of the European Union. On behalf of the EU and its member states, please, Mr. Trunin.

Thank you very much, Excellency. First, as I said earlier, all the three pillars of UN engagement are important. And one of the pillars is obviously human rights, enunciated in the very charter of the organization. At the moment, I know that expenditure on human rights is exceedingly low, so I would explore all other avenues permissible that would make it possible to increase funding for human rights activities. But that must be in the context of what I said in my remarks, that we reform the institution, we go back to the basics on the issues of human rights, and we apply them without any selectivity. That's the basis on which I would act. But I would definitely press member states to provide more resources for the work on human rights. And all the other comment that you made, Excellency, about trust, the importance of the UN Charter and the principles, international law, the importance of being clear with mandates, Absolutely, I am in agreement with those.

I thank Mr. Otunnu. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Nepal on behalf of the least developed countries, followed by the Republic of Korea, and the next or first civil society organization.

Thank you, Madam President. I have the honor to speak on behalf of the group of least developed countries, the countries that are recognized as the most structurally vulnerable. and yet the furthest behind in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. The LDC group would like to thank Mr. Otunnu for the presentation and kindly request to share his observations on the following two questions. First, if elected as Secretary-General, what will be your strategic approach to mobilize and direct adequate, predictable, and concessional resources to LDCs? And how will you reorient the UN development system so that supporting LDCs to achieve the SDGs becomes a visible system-wide priority at the country level? Second, in the face of ongoing financial constraints, how will you ensure that resources and dedicated support to LDCs, including to the LDC-dedicated UN mechanisms, are protected and strengthened rather than reduced? And what specific measures will you put in place to ring fence the support from across the board cuts? Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Nepal on behalf of the least developed countries. Please, Mr. Achuna.

Thank you, Excellency. There are two sides to this ledger. First is the responsibility of the least developed countries in the first instance to make sure that their houses are in order, that there is adequate planning, that there is local investment, mobilization of resources, that one is fighting corruption. That then provides the legitimacy, the moral grounds on which the Secretary General can go knock on other doors to mobilize the resources to support the efforts at the national level. And the knocking on doors should not only be the multilateral institutions that we know, the international financial institutions, but also there are now increasingly important role being played by the private sector. And the Secretary-General will be at your disposal to do everything he or she can to mobilize resources to support your efforts at the national level.
I thank Mr. Otunnu. I now give the floor to the Senior Representative of the Republic of Korea, also on behalf of Austria, Egypt, Ghana, Myanmar, Norway, Peru, Portugal, and Sweden.

Thank you, Madam President. Thank you, Mr. Otunnu, for joining us today. I have the privilege of delivering these questions on behalf of the nine member states, which the Norway, Sweden, Myanmar, Australia, Peru, Egypt, Ghana, the Republic Korea, and Portugal, that have had honor of having their nationals serve as the Secretary Generals of the United Nations. Drawing on our experience and the institutional memory, we wish to contribute constructively to the current selection process and stand ready to support both the process itself and the next Secretary-General. The responsibilities entrusted to the Secretary-General under the Charter are profound. While the Charter designated the Secretary-General as the chief administrative officer of the Organization, It also assigned the office an independent political role in the maintenance of international peace and security. As complex conflict continue to unfold across the globe, and calls for reform of the organization grow ever stronger, the United Nations require a Secretary General who can successfully navigate both the political and managerial dimensions of the role. equal parts of diplomat and advocate, civil servant and CEO. As a member state, they have had the honor of having their nationals serve as secretaries general. Our questions are, first, the office of the secretary general frequently require difficult judgments between principle and pragmatism, public advocacy and quiet diplomacy, action and restraint. In your course over your career, have you faced a situation in which you have to make such difficult judgment? What lessons and principles from your experiences would guide you as Secretary-General? Second, drawing on the experience of the previous Secretary-General, what lessons do you believe remain most relevant for the next Secretary-General? Thank you.
I thank the Senior Representative of the Republic of Korea on behalf of those countries having had a Secretary General. Please, Mr. Otunnu.

Thank you very much, Excellency. We must begin with principles, but we don't stop at principles. We must see what can work, what is practical, and probe and forge consensus where possible. So I do not see principles and advocacy as being in conflict. They are a continuum of action. Secondly, Excellency, yes, I have been in some very difficult situations which are very much analogous to what you are referring to. In the Security Council, I referred earlier to the deadlock of 1981. In the General Assembly, we had the crisis of Grenada in 1983. I was the chair of the Credentials Committee and had to find a way to build a consensus and to get out of that deadlock. When I was building the regime for protection of children and women in situations of conflict, same, discussing with Security Council members to incorporate this on the agenda of the Council. So, yes, I have been in such situations. I have experience of how you navigate in this difficult situation and come up with an inventive solution based on consensus you have built.
I thank Mr. Otunnu. I now give the floor to the first civil society organization, CIVICUS World Alliance for Citizens' Participation. Please, you have the floor.

Thank you for the floor. My name is Jesselina Rana, representing Civicus. Mr. Otunnu, your vision statement speaks of human rights, financing for development, environmental prosperity, and of connecting the global to the community. Yet, you do not mention civil society, an essential partner in connecting global institutions to local communities. This matters more now than ever. We are witnessing the global deterioration of civic space, anti-rights voices increasingly co-opting human rights language and UN spaces, and states continuing to flout international law and violate human rights with impunity, even as we expect a severely under-resourced human rights pillar of the UN to respond effectively to these challenges. If selected, Secretary-General, and in the spirit of We the People's What principal steps would you take to strengthen the UN's relationship with civil society, ensuring we are not simply consulted, but meaningfully engaged in shaping your leadership priorities in upholding international law? Thank you.
I thank the representative of the civil society organization, World Alliance for Citizens Participation. Please, Mr. Otunnu.

Thank you very much, Madam. I would do two things. First, The Secretary-General must do everything to reconnect the people of the world to the United Nations. The United Nations is primarily an association of member states, but the member states and the UN collectivity are acting, in the words of the Charter, in the names of the people. So the Secretary-General should promote the ideals of the UN invite the people of the world to be connected, to give them hope, give them faith. The UN should not be an ivory tower divorced from the people of the world. Secondly, you heard me say how important it is for us to move from the global to the community, enunciate aspirations and policies and values which are important. but take them down and follow them down to their impact at the national and community level. My own experience, I think I mentioned a little earlier, the last five years, I've been engaged in the womb of the community at a very difficult enterprise of rebuilding a society devastated by war and encampment. So yes, not only do I believe in this, I hope the Secretary-General will be somebody who is comfortable at all these levels, from the global to the national to the community. Thank you.
I thank Mr. Otunnu. I now give the floor to the Distinguished Representative of Austria on behalf of the Group of Friends on the Rule of Law.

Madam President, Excellencies, I have the honor to deliver this question on behalf of over 50 cross-regional members of the Group of Friends of the rule of law, and would like to thank Mr. Otuno for his presentation and answers provided so far. Excellencies, in recent years, we have witnessed breaches of even the most fundamental provisions of the UN Charter, including the obligation of all member states to refrain in the international relations from the threat or use of force, as well as mass atrocities committed at large scale in grave breach of international law. All this paired with the failure of the Security Council to take action in response. So the questions of the Group of Friends of the Rule of Law to you would be: What concrete, proactive and preventive measures would you personally pursue, if elected as Secretary-General, to strengthen the rule of law and prevent breaches by Member States of the Charter's principles and of international law? What specific preventive diplomacy initiatives would you launch or strengthen? We look forward to the exchange, and I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Austria. On behalf of the Group of Friends on the Rule of Law, please, Mr. Otuno.

Excellency, thank you very much for your question concerning not just the provisions of the UN Charter, but rule of law across the board. As I said earlier, it's very important when we're talking about norms and standards and principles which have been agreed upon at the United Nations that we should be even-handed, we should be non-selective. Nowhere is that more important than in the role of the Secretary-General, because the Secretary-General should be the custodian, the advocate, the voice for these principles and norms we are talking about in a way which is very impartial. And sometimes the Secretary General may say it publicly, other times the Secretary General may take it up quietly behind the scene. On other occasions, the Secretary General might find a way to convene a small group to discuss this. There are various instruments available to the Secretary General to perform his or her role as the chief advocate, the main voice for the norms, the principles, the rules we have agreed upon. And that would be the way I would approach this matter. Very important. Very important.
I thank Mr. Otunnu. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Lithuania on behalf of the Lublin Triangle, followed by Ukraine and the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

Thank you, Madam President. And I have the honor to speak on behalf of the Lublin Triangle, which is Poland, Ukraine, and my own country, Lithuania. Russia's ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine continues to undermine the foundation of the international rules-based order. It has been accompanied by credible and well-documented reports of serious violations of international humanitarian and human rights law, including the deportation of children, widespread attacks against civilian infrastructure, and arbitrary detention. These acts are not isolated incidents, but rather form patterns that demand a consistent and principled international response. At the same time, this situation has exposed important limitations within the current multilateral system. While a range of UN bodies and international mechanisms have been mobilized, challenges remain in ensuring effective coordination, preserving evidence, and ultimately delivering accountability. Strengthening collective actions across institutions is therefore essential to prevent impunity, uphold international law, and maintain trust in the UN system. Against this background, we would like to raise the following questions. How can coordination between the Security Council, the ICC, the General Assembly and other UN bodies be improved to help prevent impunity? How can UN better support cooperation with international and national investigations to document and preserve evidence of war crimes in Ukraine? What practical role can the Secretary-General and his good offices play in supporting the implementation of General Assembly resolutions, such as the resolution Return of Ukrainian Children of 3 December 2025, and advancing accountability in this situation? I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative from Lithuania. On behalf of the Lublin Triangle, please, Mr. Otunio.

I thank you, Excellency, for your question. The Security Council of the United Nations, the ICC, and all other entities of the UN which deal with standards and rules and resolutions of the UN should not accept impunity, should do everything to stop or discourage impunity. So that is clear, and it's not just for the ICC, the Security Council, for all the UN bodies. Secondly, I think you've heard me say explicitly that among the situations of conflict that I would address right away, engage in right away, see what the UN can do, would be the situation in Ukraine. I have also said, you heard me say earlier, that one of the most disturbing scenarios today is seeing that in all these conflicts, children, women, innocent people are suffering unbelievably. It's another reason why we cannot be indifferent. We must do everything to try to bring these conflicts to an end because the toll, the tragedy on innocent people is unacceptable.
I thank Mr. Otunnu. I now give the floor to the Skinglish representative of Ogri on behalf of the Group of 77 and China.

Thank you, Madam President. The group attaches great importance to the selection and appointment of the Secretary General and reaffirms the need to ensure that this process remains open, transparent, and inclusive in accordance with the relevant General Assembly resolutions. In this regard, we wish to raise the following questions to Mr. Otunnu. First, on the UN initiative introduced by the Secretary General, Antonio Guterres, what is your assessment of the proposal and how do you believe it could advance a UN that is more effective, efficient and delivers greater impact on the ground? How would you ensure that any related reforms fully respect the intergovernmental nature of the UN, preserve the balance among its three pillars and do not come at the expense of development mandates or other priorities of developing countries? Second, on financing for development, how would you, as Secretary-General, mobilize the UN system to defend and advance the development pillar, accelerate implementation of the 2030 Agenda, and support financing for development in a manner fully responsive to the priorities of developing countries, particularly at a time of shrinking fiscal space, declining ODA, rising debt burdens, and widening development gaps? Third, on geographical and gender balance, how How would you, as Secretary-General, ensure equal and fair distribution based on gender and geographical balance, as prescribed by Article 101 of the Charter and the relevant General Assembly resolutions, particularly in terms of the overall increase in the representation of unrepresented and underrepresented countries, especially from developing countries, at the senior level appointments within the UN Secretariat and the broader UN system? Fourth, on the UN financial situation, what concrete measures would you, as Secretary-General, undertake to promote compliance with Member States' financial obligations and ensure that assessed contributions are paid in full on time and without conditions, particularly in light of the record level of arrears owed to the Organization? Madam President, the Group of 77 and China underscores the importance of safeguarding the full independence, impartiality and institutional integrity of the Secretariat, while ensuring the provision of equitable and effective support to the representations of all Member States in the discharge of their responsibilities. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of OGRY. On behalf of the Group of 77 and China, please, Mr. Otunov.

I thank you, Excellency. The Secretary General and the Secretariat must always be impartial, independent, respectful of member states, and listening patiently to the member states, and of course implementing the decisions of the member states. It is very important, Excellency, that the United Nations should be the United Nations of inclusion. The United Nations should, even in its bureaucracy, look like the world it represents. So it is very important that whether in terms of geography, in terms of cultures, in terms of gender, The UN should look like the world it represents. It should be very inclusive. Financing for development, as I said earlier, and also in my little vision statement, I elaborate on this, that first, I insist the responsibility begins at the national level, that the national authorities should assume responsibility for their development and do the right thing. Then the Secretary-General can help to knock on doors that can bring more resources, and not just those which have been part of the official multilateral development funding or even bilateral development funding. There are other possible sources now available, and the Secretary-General should knock on all of them to mobilize resources for countries which have done well to put in place the plan, the arrangements for their development. On the issue of reform, reform, as I said earlier, is no longer an option, it is an imperative. But reform is an imperative precisely because we want the good work which the UN has done in the past and continues to do now to continue. Reform should not be the ending of multilateralism, but the strengthening of multilateralism to make it more effective, have more impact, and have the U.N. of service. That is the purpose of reform. And it's also the reason why it mustn't be a project determined in time, but an attitude change, a transformation, a new culture that we install within the U.N. system. And then, finally, I say that U.N. 80 is a wonderful basis on which to conduct reform. A good deal has been done. Much more needs to be done. We need to deepen what we should do. We need to consolidate programs and activities. We need to look more carefully at mandates to make sure that they are clear, that there are resources for carrying them out. There's a whole range of things we can put. But let me just say finally, Excellencies, that in my experience, We could agree on five or six things which are critical to be done, experts and member states and the bureaucracy. But I think what has been lacking perhaps is the will to carry through what we have agreed upon. I thank Mr. Otunnu. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Kingdom of the Netherlands on behalf of the Benelux Union, followed by the next civil society organization and Andorra.

Thank you, Madam President, and I thank Mr. Otunnu for sharing his vision. We align with the statement delivered by the European Union. We attach particular importance to a Secretary-General who, one, can strengthen trust in multilateralism and the international legal order, and two, who can act as a strong convening power across all three pillars. and three, who can proactively contribute to prevention, peacebuilding, and mediation. At the same time, we see a need to strengthen the UN's financial sustainability, accountability, and system-wide coherence. We place high value on leadership that can connect the UN's development work with broader efforts on peace, security, and human rights particularly in times of systemic stress. In your vision, Mr. Otunnu, you state that the next Secretary-General should shepherd genuine and lasting reforms, with Member States taking responsibility for coherent mandate creation, implementation, and review. What concrete steps would you take to encourage Member States to align mandates with resources and to reduce application while preserving the UN's ability to respond to emerging needs. Finally, Mr. Otunnu, could you kindly share your early thinking on the composition of your senior leadership team, including the Deputy Secretary-General? How would you approach considerations such as regional balance, gender, and the specific qualities needed to support your priorities? Thank you.

Thank you, Excellency. First, on the team around me, I would ensure that I have the most talented team possible, and that that team reflects the membership the cultures, the geography that compose the United Nations. Fortunately, talent is available across the globe, so that should be possible to do. On the issue of power and the role of the Secretary-General, let me just say this. I say it in my vision statement. And the Secretary-General does not wield conventional power. That is by design. The Secretary-General has soft power that flows from two streams. The first is the principles of the Charter. He or she is the guardian of the principles of the Charter. And the second stream is the support of member states. When the Secretary-General has these two, he or she has soft power, a platform on which to do some important things. I said earlier that reform should not be the ending of multilateralism. On the contrary. reform should strengthen multilateralism and give it the legitimacy it needs now and the capacity to deliver better on the function, the role that is set out for the UN in the Charter. In terms of my leadership, I think everywhere where I've had the opportunity, whether within the UN or outside the UN, I brought a certain amount of rigor. I brought a certain amount of making sure that those who may have competing views are brought together. I put particular premium on coming up, not being shy, to propose inventive and innovative solutions.

Thank you.
I thank Mr. Ochunolu. I now give the floor to the next civil society organization, the Light Millennium Charter Global Human Advancement Organization. Please, you have the floor.

Madam President, Excellencies, and Mr. Candidate, the UN Charter promises sovereign equality to all nations. The next Secretary-General will play a critical role, not only in defending the UN Charter, but also in reinvigorating and reshaping the role and relevance of the UN. And we as small states look to the Secretary-General to safeguard the interests of all member states, not just the big major powers and the permanent members, but to look after, in particular, the interests of the smallest, weakest, and most vulnerable members of the UN. We do not want a world of might is right, where international law and the sovereignty and territorial integrity of small states are violated with impunity. Thank you very much, Excellency. If I may say so, Excellency, you know, the UN as a multilateral institution is not only crucial for small states, I think it is important for all of us. That is why any reform we carry out should be to strengthen multilateralism, not to kill it. We shouldn't throw away the baby with the water in our reform project. So the sentiment you feel as small states, I think most member states feel, let us work together to rescue multilateralism, strengthen it, reform the institution. Secondly, the importance of international law. Absolutely, absolutely. I strongly believe in that. I've contributed to that at various levels. I've taught that in various universities. It's very important for me personally and important to this institution. Now, you ask about the General Assembly and the Security Council. You know the way this institution is designed, perhaps we should make the mistake. The General Assembly cannot take the place of the Security Council. Each have their role well defined within the Charter. But what we should promote, what the Secretary General should encourage is cooperation between the two bodies, not conflict, not one taking over from the other. That is the way I would approach this. On SDGs, we are not on track to achieve what has been promulgated. I hope we can improve. And if I was elected Secretary-General, I would make this a priority because the SDGs are very, very important to our development agenda, especially for the developing countries. And again, as I said earlier, countries must do their homework and be good custodian of the development agenda. And I would be ready to do that.

And also because of the unbelievable suffering these visits on innocent people. That is why I have flagged the major conflicts going on now as a particular priority of the Secretary General. But all the three pillars are important, we must continue to work on all of them. Now, in terms of resources, it is not easy, and there is no easy answer. What is clear is that the UN is under enormous pressure. It can't carry all this burden. It is the reason why the UN should very intentionally work in partnership with other actors, especially regional organizations. When the UN was founded, there were barely any regional organizations. Thank God today there are several regional organizations, and some have played very useful and very important roles. They should be encouraged. They should be empowered. There should be partnership and cooperation between the UN and the regional bodies. And the UN should also reach out to other actors when we speak about, for example, artificial intelligence, the private sector, technology companies are very important in this. They should be at the table. They should have their say at the table. And this goes for climate change. It can go for other areas of UN activities as well, which should be more open. open to others and they open to us.

Indeed, when we are involved in reform as we are now, we should take into account the views, the perspectives of Member States, of the staff of the United Nations. So the UN staff, their views, their role, and cooperation between the UN Secretariat and the membership is very important. I have the experience of working with them all in difficult and not so difficult situations. I can draw on that. We cannot go very far if there is no trust, whether between the Secretary-General and Member States, between the Security Council and the General Assembly, between the staff and Member States. The Secretary-General is the go-between. He or she must make sure that trust is restored, that we are one house and moving in the same direction with common interests for humanity. Very, very important, not easy, but very important.

Excellency, I was there when the resolution on the right to development was adopted. Development is very important, is one of the three pillars of UN action. And I would support that fully. It affects a large swath of the membership of the UN and of the population of the world. So we must not in any way relent in our efforts to promote development. And that is why the fate of the SDGs are very important. I've already commented on that. I've commented on the rule of law, all aspects of the rule of law. The Secretary General should encourage member states and all concerned to conduct themselves in accordance with the charter of the United Nations, in accordance with the principles of the United Nations which have been agreed upon, and in accordance with the norms which have been developed and agreed by the United Nations. That is the role of the Secretary General. He or she didn't make the principles, doesn't make them up, but invokes promotes and encourages the application of those principles and those norms.

Thank you, Madam President, for convening this interactive dialogue. Excellency, mediation, good offices, the go-between, facilitating, convening role of the Secretary-General is capital. That is what the Secretary-General is there for. Conflict resolution and mediation happen today more and more outside UN official structures and without UN mandate. What could the new UN Secretary-General do to better prevent and resolve violent conflicts? And what is the role of civil society in all of this?

I thank you, Excellency. When I was involved in developing the regime for the protection of children affected by war, I visited many conflict situations. I met with civil society groups. I met with parties in conflict, those which may be state actors, non-state actors, all of them. So I have some deep experience how to insert the UN in a way which is appropriate, be of service, and help the parties in conflict or help those who are contesting a particular situation. Secondly, I know that preventing conflict is easier said than done, in part because even when the signs are there, the parties in conflict may be in denial. Nevertheless, it is the role of the Secretary-General to be engaged, to be prodding, to be suggesting, to be calling attention to what requires action. This, perhaps, you know, good offices, mediation, being a facilitator, convener, is one of the most important roles of the Secretary-General and is part of the soft power of the Secretary-General to which I referred earlier.

In terms of what the Pact for the Future says about Africa's outlook on reform of the Security Council, perhaps, you know, Africa outlook is partly determined by what is viewed by Africa as a historical imbalance. But as I said earlier, reforming the Security Council is not the The primary role doesn't belong to the Secretary-General, even though the Secretary-General should encourage, should draw attention to factors to be taken into account, and should try to encourage some kind of a consensus to emerge. Excellency, first, the Secretary-General should always invoke the Charter. the principles of the Charter, regardless of the situation, in a way which is impartial, in a way which is equal, and a way which is responsible. And secondly, in the case of particular countries in need, as I said earlier, when they have done their own homework and their own planning and their own mobilization of resources domestically and fighting corruption, it's for the Secretary-General to knock on certain doors on their behalf. And secondly, it's also, I think, important that in terms of advocacy, the Secretary-General should continue to be a key advocate. And thirdly, I would say this, I think I said it earlier, that for me it's very important the UN shouldn't be a diplomatic ivory tower. The SDGs are important, I believe in them, but we should now follow the trail of the SDGs as they go to national and to community levels to make sure that we are connected, that we have the same understanding, and that these things will in fact produce the results we want. I don't have time to give you examples of how some of the Millennium Development Goals that I was very much involved in went wrong in terms of implementation at the national and local levels. should guard against that.
